climate.fall: September-early October: Shorter daylight and increasing freeze-thaw cycles create unstable snow/ice conditions. First snow possible. Days are cooler (40-60°F); nights regularly below freezing. Weather windows are shorter and less predictable.
climate.spring: May-June: Winter-like conditions persist; significant snow coverage aids glacier travel but avalanche hazard is elevated and icefalls are common. Extreme variability with potential for warm sunny days followed by storms. Bergschrunds are wide and difficult to cross.
climate.summer: July-August: Warmest season with daytime temperatures 50-70°F at lower elevations; above 8,000 ft expect 30-50°F days and 20-30°F nights. Morning sun creates firm snow (especially valuable for glacier travel); afternoon heating increases rockfall and avalanche hazard. Afternoon thunderstorms common; rain possible even mid-summer.
climate.winter: November-April: Heavy snow adds distance and complexity; avalanche hazard is significant. Requires backcountry skiing skills. Temperature inversions create extreme cold at altitude (well below 0°F at night). Winter traverse option via ski requires specialized skills and is rarely attempted.
climate.typical: Highly variable, rapidly changing weather is the norm. Summer (July-August) features warm daytime temperatures (50-70°F at lower elevations, 30-50°F at altitude), cold nights (freezing to 20°F), and strong UV exposure. Afternoon thunderstorms are common; mornings are typically clearer. Humidity is high, creating fog and mist frequent in upper elevations.
climate.forecastZone: Northwest Avalanche Center (NWAC) Cascades zone; weather forecasts available via NOAA forecast for North Cascades region

climate.typical: Wet, snowy winters (Nov–Apr) with lingering snowpack at Marmot Pass and on the summit slopes often into July; summers (Jul–Sep) bring the reliable snow-free window, with warm days, cool nights, and afternoon convective/thunderstorm risk on the exposed ridge and summit.

bySeason.fall: September–October is generally stable and dry but with shorter days and the possibility of an early season storm at elevation.
bySeason.spring: Trail is often snow-covered above roughly 4,500 ft into June, and creek crossings run high with snowmelt.
bySeason.summer: July–September is typically snow-free at the pass and summit; wildflower bloom peaks in July. Carry sun protection — there's minimal shade above treeline.
bySeason.winter: Heavy snow and avalanche terrain on the approach slopes make this a mountaineering objective in winter, not a scramble; requires avalanche assessment and gear.

climate.spring: Heavy lingering snowpack on the route's upper slopes and ridge into June; the approach trail may still carry snow at elevation.
climate.summer: Primary climbing season (Jul–Sep); warm and generally dry but prone to sudden afternoon convective storms.
climate.winter: Deep snowpack and avalanche terrain on the approach and route; the access road is not maintained for winter travel this far up-valley.
climate.typical: Dry east-slope Cascades climate - less precipitation and more sun than the west-side range - but the trail follows the shaded Entiat River bottom for many miles before opening into Entiat Meadows.

bySeason.fall: Short, clear weather windows with cold nights; larches turn gold in nearby basins in late September/October, but the road can see early snow.
bySeason.spring: Entiat River Road may still be gated below the trailhead; the upper mountain holds steep, corniced snow - full mountaineering gear required, not a scramble.
bySeason.summer: Best window; usually snow-free scrambling by August, but expect heavy mosquitoes in Entiat Meadows through July and lingering icy snow in the summit gully into early July.
bySeason.winter: Road gated well below the trailhead; full winter conditions on the peak.

climate.forecastZone: East-slope Entiat/Chelan Mountains - outside NWAC's core coverage zones; use NWAC's nearest east-slope Central Cascades forecast as a rough reference and rely on direct observation for spring snow conditions.

climate.fall: Prime season with cool, generally stable weather; western larches turn gold late September-mid October, drawing the year's heaviest crowds.
climate.spring: Trail and access road typically remain snowed in through May-June; not recommended.
climate.summer: Warm and mostly dry July-August, with lingering snow possible into July on shaded upper switchbacks and occasional afternoon thunderstorms.
climate.winter: Access road (FR 6211/FR 6200) unmaintained and typically snowed in by November-December; not a winter objective.
climate.typical: Dry, sunny east-Cascades rain-shadow climate typical of the Chiwawa/Entiat drainages — noticeably less precipitation and more settled summer weather than the west-side Cascades, though afternoon thunderstorms and early-season snow at this elevation (into September/October) do occur.

bySeason.fall: Famous golden larch season in late September–early October, by far the busiest time on the trail.
bySeason.spring: Snow lingers on the upper trail into early summer, and the access road (FR 6200/6211) is typically not reliably open until roughly June.
bySeason.summer: Wildflower meadows and prime hiking July–August; afternoon thunderstorms possible.
bySeason.winter: Access road unmaintained/snow-closed; reaching the trailhead requires skis or snowshoes from a lower closure point.

climate.forecastZone: Not within a core NWAC-forecast zone — the Entiat Mountains/Chiwawa drainage sit east of NWAC's published zones (e.g. Stevens Pass); for winter travel, use general regional trends from the nearest NWAC zone plus Okanogan-Wenatchee NF advisories rather than a zone-specific forecast.

climate.typical: East-of-the-crest transitional climate: drier and sunnier than the west-side Cascades but still exposed to Pacific frontal systems. Afternoon thunderstorms are common in summer, and the high-latitude border-country position keeps nights cool even in July/August.

bySeason.fall: Stable high pressure is common but days shorten fast; early snow can arrive by October in a heavier-snow year (though a low-snow-year October ascent has been documented).
bySeason.spring: Deep snowpack lingers into July at this elevation and latitude; the Freezeout Creek Trail and upper slopes are typically snowbound.
bySeason.summer: Prime window (late July-September); long daylight but watch for afternoon convective storms building over the Pasayten crest.
bySeason.winter: Full winter conditions; SR-20 and Silver-Skagit Road both closed, making the peak effectively inaccessible.

climate.fall: September is the quality window — cold, stable, bug-free air and firm rock, but short days and the first autumn storms. Snow can fall on the peak at any time of year.
climate.spring: Not a practical season. Snow lies deep on the approach trails and the Chewuch/Andrews Creek roads and trailheads are snowbound; the Forest Service gives October–May as the snow season.
climate.summer: Prime season. Eastern-side trails are typically clear by early July; days are long and warm, afternoon thunderstorms build regularly over the Okanogan crest, and mosquitoes near Upper Cathedral Lake are severe through mid-August.
climate.winter: Effectively off-limits: unplowed roads plus 17–22 miles of snow-covered approach, and no avalanche forecast product covers the Pasayten.
climate.typical: Dry continental east-slope climate — markedly sunnier and less stormy than the western North Cascades, with hot valley days, cool nights at 7,400 ft camp elevation and strong summer diurnal convection over the crest.
climate.forecastZone: NWS Spokane point forecast for 48.99 N / -120.19 W (Okanogan County); call the Methow Valley Ranger District at (509) 996-4000 for trail and snow conditions. No mountain-specific commercial forecast product covers this peak.

climate.fall: September is the connoisseur's month — cold, stable, bug-free, and quiet, but with short days and the first snowfalls possible. Lower trails see hunting season traffic.
climate.spring: Impractical — the roads and the 17+ mile approach are snowbound; Forest Service snow season is October–May.
climate.summer: Prime. Trails clear by early July on the east side; the southwest aspect melts out first. Long days, afternoon thunderstorms, and severe mosquitoes near the lakes into mid-August.
climate.winter: Not a practical objective: unplowed roads and 17–22 miles of snow-covered approach.
climate.typical: Dry east-slope continental climate: warm sunny days, cold nights at the 7,380 ft camp, afternoon convection over the crest, and far less rain than the western North Cascades.
climate.forecastZone: NWS Spokane point forecast for 48.99 N / -120.19 W (Okanogan County); Methow Valley Ranger District (509) 996-4000 for trail and snow conditions.

climate.fall: September gives the best rock and the most stable air of the year. New snow can arrive from late September.
climate.spring: Snow route conditions and avalanche potential on the approach slopes; road and trail snowbound.
climate.summer: The climbing season. Shade on the buttress is welcome in August heat, but afternoon thunderstorms over the crest are the main hazard.
climate.winter: Snowbound; no practical vehicle access and effectively no traffic.
climate.typical: Marine west coast climate; heavy orographic winter precipitation on the crest, drier and clearer summers under Pacific high pressure. This northeast aspect stays in shade until late morning.
climate.forecastZone: Northwest Avalanche Center (nwac.us) — Snoqualmie Pass zone, cross-referenced with East Slopes Central for the Cle Elum drainage; relevant for the approach snowfield in spring and early summer.

climate.fall: September offers the driest rock and the most stable air of the year — the best time for a route with marginal protection. Snow returns from late September.
climate.spring: Snowbound approach and avalanche potential; road closed or muddy. Not a rock season.
climate.summer: The climbing season, with afternoon convective thunderstorms the principal weather hazard on an exposed ridge.
climate.winter: Snowbound and inaccessible by vehicle.
climate.typical: Marine west coast climate: heavy orographic winter precipitation over the crest, drier and clearer summers under Pacific high pressure. The northeast aspect is shaded until late morning and dries slowly.
climate.forecastZone: Northwest Avalanche Center (nwac.us) — Snoqualmie Pass zone, with East Slopes Central for the drier Cle Elum drainage snowpack.

climate.fall: September gives the driest slab conditions and the most stable weather of the year; new snow can arrive from late September.
climate.spring: Full snow route with avalanche potential; the approach road and trail are snowbound.
climate.summer: The climbing season, but this aspect melts out later than the rest of the peak — expect snow in the couloir into July.
climate.winter: Snowbound and inaccessible by road.
climate.typical: Marine west coast climate with heavy orographic winter precipitation on the crest and comparatively dry, clear summers under Pacific high pressure. This northwest aspect sits in shade for much of the day.
climate.forecastZone: Northwest Avalanche Center (nwac.us) — Snoqualmie Pass zone, with East Slopes Central for the east-side snowpack in the Cle Elum drainage. Particularly relevant for this route, which is a snow climb early in the season.

climate.fall: Cold, stable, clear stretches in September are the best conditions of the year: dry rock, no bugs, and long shadows on the tower. Storms return in earnest by October and snow can arrive on the summit any time from late September.
climate.spring: Deep, wet snowpack low down and continuing storms. FR 4330 is snowbound or muddy, the trail is under snow above the forest, and avalanche hazard exists on the steep flanks and in the gullies. Not a rock season.
climate.summer: Pacific high pressure builds and summers are typically clear and warm. This is the climbing season. Afternoon convective thunderstorms are the main summer weather hazard, especially in July and August.
climate.winter: Snowbound and effectively inaccessible for climbing. The road is unplowed past Salmon la Sac and the peak sees very little winter traffic.
climate.typical: Marine west coast regime: Pacific weather systems track inland and are forced up over the Cascades (orographic lift), dropping heavy precipitation on the crest. Cathedral Rock sits just east of the crest, so it is measurably drier and sunnier than the west-slope peaks but still catches crest weather.
climate.forecastZone: Northwest Avalanche Center (nwac.us) covers the central Washington Cascades here; read the Snoqualmie Pass zone and, for the drier east-side snowpack in the Cle Elum drainage, the East Slopes Central discussion. NWS Pendleton/Seattle point forecasts and mountain-forecast style summit forecasts are the usual supplements.

climate.fall: September into early October brings the most stable weather of the year, cool climbing, quiet trails and larches at the bench camp - offset by short days, a cold east face with only morning sun, and open moats at the snow-rock margin.
climate.spring: Out of season. SR 20 is typically gated, the approach gully and traverse are full snow travel with avalanche potential, and the east face is cold and often damp in the corner systems.
climate.summer: The season. Late June through August gives dry cracks and long days, though the col gully holds snow into early summer and the traverse beneath Burgundy's east face carries snow year-round. Early starts are essential for firm snow and for beating afternoon convection.
climate.winter: Access is closed with SR 20; the approach is avalanche terrain and the route is not a realistic winter objective.
climate.typical: Dry east-slope Cascade climate in the crest's rain shadow - fast-drying rock and frequent settled high pressure, with clear mornings that often build into afternoon thunderstorms over the Silver Star cirque.
climate.forecastZone: Okanogan County, eastern North Cascades. Use the NOAA/NWS point forecast for Washington Pass and the Northwest Avalanche Center's Washington Pass and Mazama weather stations for shoulder-season snow information; elevation-band forecasts for Silver Star Mountain cover the same cirque.

climate.fall: September into early October is often the most stable and pleasant window - cool, dry air and firm ground - at the cost of short days, cold shade on the north side, and thin, melted-out snow with wide moats at the rock margin.
climate.spring: Snow-covered and generally out of season. SR 20 is usually still closed; when it opens, the approach gully to Burgundy Col and the traverse under Burgundy's east face are full winter/spring snow travel with avalanche potential, and the rock routes are wet and cold.
climate.summer: The season. Late June through August gives warm, mostly dry days, though the approach gully holds snow into early summer and the traverse under Burgundy Spire carries snow year-round. Start early to be off the exposed summit before afternoon convection and to catch the col gully while the snow is firm.
climate.winter: SR 20 is gated closed across Washington Pass, removing practical access. The approach gully below Burgundy Col is avalanche terrain and the spires are not a realistic winter objective from this side.
climate.typical: Dry east-slope Cascade climate. The Wine Spires sit far enough east of the crest to escape much of the maritime weather that plagues the western North Cascades, so the rock dries fast and settled high-pressure spells are common. The dominant summer hazard is convective: clear mornings that build into afternoon thunderstorms over the Silver Star cirque.
climate.forecastZone: Okanogan County, eastern North Cascades. Use the NOAA/NWS point forecast for Washington Pass and the Northwest Avalanche Center's Washington Pass and Mazama weather stations for shoulder-season snow and avalanche information; elevation-band forecasts for Silver Star Mountain cover the same cirque.

climate.typical: Maritime Cascades climate; winters bring deep, wet snowpack (peaking March–April), summers are drier with the most reliable snow-free window from early/mid-July through October.

bySeason.fall: Good clear window with fall color, fewer bugs, and easier stream crossings
bySeason.spring: Snow-covered gully and approach trail; avalanche risk on the gully and ridge
bySeason.summer: Best window — dry talus and scree by August in most years
bySeason.winter: Full snow cover, trailhead roads may be gated

climate.fall: Early fall (September into early October) can be excellent — cool, stable, and quiet — but Pacific storm systems return and daylight shortens quickly. After early October, plan for rain and snow.
climate.spring: Wet and snowy on the upper mountain. Avalanche conditions persist into the NWAC forecast season's end in mid-April, the valley trail is muddy with high river flows, and the trailhead road may still be gated.
climate.summer: The season. July through September gives the driest rock and the most stable weather; snow can still linger on the upper mountain into early July after a big winter. Expect warm, buggy rainforest on the approach and much cooler conditions on the summit ridge.
climate.winter: Full winter conditions with deep snow, short days, and a gated approach road. NWAC's Olympics zone runs avalanche forecasts through this period. A winter ascent would be a serious expedition, not a variation.
climate.typical: Marine west coast climate. Heavy precipitation, much of it as winter snow at elevation, and frequent low cloud and rain even in summer. June through September is the only reliably favourable window for climbing here.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC 'Olympics' avalanche forecast zone (forecasts issued daily at 6 pm, roughly mid-November through mid-April); NOAA/NWS Seattle point forecast for the summit coordinates.

climate.typical: Wet maritime climate near the crest; clearest and driest mid- to late summer.

bySeason.fall: Short window; bergschrund and crevasses open
bySeason.spring: Snow-covered; glacier well filled, avalanche risk
bySeason.summer: Prime window; rock dries and glacier firms overnight
bySeason.winter: Full winter alpine conditions, rarely climbed

climate.forecastZone: No dedicated NWAC zone covers this peak; nearest approximate coverage is the Stevens Pass / East Slopes Central zone boundary (Alpine Lakes crest near Cooper Lake).

climate.typical: East-slope North Cascades climate: drier and sunnier than the west-side crest, but the elevation still holds a substantial snowpack into summer; afternoon thunderstorms are common in July-August.

bySeason.fall: Good stable weather often persists into September/early October, then increasing chance of new snow at elevation.
bySeason.spring: Full snow cover on the approach and upper mountain; avalanche hazard on slopes near the col; Chiwawa River Road usually still gated or snowed in.
bySeason.summer: Prime season; snow retreats from the trail and lower slopes by July, though the col and upper ridge can hold snow into July in heavy years.
bySeason.winter: Road closed/snowed in; full winter mountaineering conditions, essentially inaccessible.

climate.fall: Early to mid-September gives excellent friction, cool temperatures and larch colour around Colchuck Lake, at the cost of short days that make a car-to-car push tight. Weather turns unsettled quickly from late September, and the first storms end the season.
climate.spring: Snow-bound and inaccessible. FR 7601 is normally closed through May, the trail to Colchuck Lake is under snow, and the approach gully and west basin are full avalanche terrain. Not a climbing season.
climate.summer: The season. Late July and August are the recommended window: dry rock, minimal seepage, and cool west-facing shade that makes the wall pleasant even during hot spells in Leavenworth. Early July still means seepage under the roofs and snow in the approach gully. Afternoon convective build-up is the main day-to-day risk.
climate.winter: Not a climbing season for these rock routes. Deep snow, road closure, avalanche-prone approach terrain and severe cold; the wall is a winter alpine objective for no one.
climate.typical: Pacific weather systems are forced upward by the Cascade crest and drop most of their moisture on the west side, so the Stuart Range sits partly in the rain shadow: winters are cloudy and stormy, while summer high pressure brings little or no cloud cover. The west aspect of the wall keeps it in shade all morning and in sun through the afternoon.
climate.forecastZone: No summer avalanche product covers this terrain — NWAC issues Cascade east-slopes zone forecasts only from roughly mid-November through mid-April. Summer parties should use the NOAA/NWS point forecast for the Colchuck Lake area of the Stuart Range and a mountain-specific forecast for the summit elevation.

climate.typical: East of the Cascade crest, so drier and sunnier than west-slope North Cascades peaks, but still cold and snowy at 7,000+ ft; the Southeast Glacier remnant and approach snowfields persist well into summer.

climate.fall: Cool, dry and often stable in a good year, but the couloir is at its most stripped and the days are short for a two-day climb finishing with a 6,000-ft forest descent.
climate.spring: The most attractive window for the face. Late winter and early spring keep the couloir filled and frozen, the lower rock band icy rather than bare slab, the bergschrund closed, and the slide alder on the approach rib leafless. Watch for wet-loose and wet-slab release on the sun-hit south-facing descent by early afternoon.
climate.summer: The couloir loses its ice; the first ascent went in July, so the line still goes as a rock-and-snow route at mid-fifth class on the lower band. The south-side descent becomes an oven and its water sources dry up, and the approach brush is at full leaf.
climate.winter: Ascents have been made. The one recorded winter ascent was 13 March 2005; a party on the south side climbed in January and recorded -22F at the 5,720-ft saddle. Expect deep snow, very large cornices along the summit ridge, and daylight that is the limiting factor on the descent.
climate.typical: West-side maritime North Cascades. Pacific fronts drive heavy orographic precipitation onto these slopes, giving deep winter snow and significant rain in the other seasons. The base of the mountain is only about 1,100 ft above sea level while the summit is 7,054 ft, so the snowline moves through nearly 6,000 ft of relief and conditions on the approach can be completely different from conditions on the face.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC West Slopes North (avalanche); NOAA/NWS Seattle point forecast for the Diablo Dam quadrangle

climate.fall: Cool and often settled, but the lack of water can make it an ordeal and the days are short for a 6,000-ft trailless climb plus descent.
climate.spring: The recommended window. Snow suppresses the salal and slide alder, snowmelt supplies water on an otherwise dry slope, and avalanche danger on the south side is minimal. Expect the snow to go to mush on this aspect by early afternoon on a sunny day.
climate.summer: Hot and dry. The route is almost entirely south-facing and would be an oven in mid-summer; water disappears and the brush is at full leaf. This is the season nobody recommends.
climate.winter: Done, and arguably one of the better times if you can handle the cold: the brush is buried. One party climbed it over the first weekend in January, camping in sub-zero conditions at the 5,720+ ft saddle down to -22F, and passed huge cornices on the summit crest. Snowshoes to the saddle; leave them there for the summit push.
climate.typical: West-side maritime North Cascades — Pacific fronts, heavy orographic precipitation, considerable snow in winter and significant rain the rest of the year. The route spans nearly 6,000 ft of relief on one aspect, so the top and the bottom are frequently in different weather.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC West Slopes North (avalanche); NOAA/NWS Seattle point forecast for the Diablo Dam quadrangle

climate.fall: September: Cooling nights, shorter days, lower crowds. Early September resembles summer; late September sees increasing snow risk. October can have early snow on high terrain.
climate.spring: April–May: Snow lingers on approach gullies above 3,500 ft through May; ice axe often needed. Spring runoff swells creeks. Approach is technical and avalanche-hazardous early in season.
climate.summer: June–August: Most reliable climbing window. June is typically drier than July–August. Expect afternoon clouds and occasional thunderstorms. July–August can be humid and buggy. Water is abundant in approach gullies.
climate.winter: November–March: Route is snow and ice-covered; winter alpine climbing required. Approach is avalanche-hazardous. Not recommended for most climbers.
climate.typical: The Central-West Cascades are maritime-influenced with mild summers and wet winters. Expect rapidly changing weather, afternoon thunderstorms (especially July–August), and cool nights. Afternoon clouds and rain are common even in summer.

climate.fall: Short days and returning rain; a dry September spell can work but leaves little daylight margin.
climate.spring: Snow in the gullies and soaked brush; the loose/mossy gully rock is at its most dangerous.
climate.summer: July-September is the window. Long days are essential — this is a 12-16 hour objective from the car.
climate.winter: Not an objective — unplowed road, wet heavy snowpack, avalanche-prone gullies.
climate.typical: Marine west coast: wet and snowy most of the year with a short dry mid-summer window. Garfield's low elevation means brush and dirt, not snow, are the seasonal problem.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC Snoqualmie Pass zone (west slopes central Washington Cascades)

climate.fall: Cool and dry spells can be excellent but the days are too short for a comfortable descent.
climate.spring: Water running down the face and snow in the upper gullies; slabs are wet and the runout sections unjustifiable.
climate.summer: July-September, after a dry spell. Long days matter for the descent over the West Peak.
climate.winter: Out of condition — snow, wet avalanche hazard, unplowed access road.
climate.typical: Marine west coast climate, heavy precipitation outside a short summer dry window; south-facing slabs dry relatively fast after a storm but the streaks run late into the season.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC Snoqualmie Pass zone (west slopes central Washington Cascades)

climate.fall: A dry early-autumn window can work but the 15-hour day no longer fits in the daylight.
climate.spring: Snow in the upper gullies and saturated brush and dirt — the route's terrain is at its most dangerous.
climate.summer: July through September, after several dry days. The longest days of summer are effectively part of the gear list.
climate.winter: Snow-covered, avalanche-prone and accessed by an unplowed road; not a winter route.
climate.typical: Marine west coast climate with very high annual precipitation; the route's dirt, brush, heather and mossy gully rock all need an extended dry spell before the climb is reasonable.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC Snoqualmie Pass zone (west slopes central Washington Cascades)

climate.fall: Cool temperatures are pleasant but the days are short and the first autumn storms re-wet the slabs and heather for the season.
climate.spring: Snow lingers in the gullies and the brush and dirt stay saturated; the scramble terrain is genuinely dangerous when not dry.
climate.summer: July through September is the season; long daylight matters as much as the weather because these routes are 12-16 hour days.
climate.winter: Snow-covered, avalanche-prone wet snowpack, and an unplowed access road. Not a winter objective.
climate.typical: Marine west coast climate — very high precipitation, mostly as heavy wet snow in winter, with a short reliable dry window in mid to late summer. Because Garfield is low and brushy, its routes hold water long after the weather clears.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC Snoqualmie Pass zone (west slopes central Washington Cascades)

climate.fall: September-October sees transition; increasing rainfall and cooler temps. October typically gets 3+ inches precipitation.
climate.spring: May-June sees increasing temperatures and lower snowpack. Rainfall decreases as summer approaches. Expect 60-65F highs.
climate.summer: July-September best for climbing. July driest (0.74 in precip), highs 73-74F. August warmer but coastal fog (foggust). September still stable, highs 68F.
climate.winter: November-April: wet, cold, snowy at elevation. Unsafe for sport climbing due to ice, snow, and frequent storms.
climate.typical: Cool maritime climate; summers dry with marine fog possibility. Winters wet with frequent precipitation. Lower elevation climbing area sees less snow than higher peaks.
climate.forecastZone: Olympic Mountains / North Olympic Peninsula (NOAA Zone WAZ328)

climate.fall: Cool temperatures and the best friction of the year; short days matter little on a 50-foot route.
climate.spring: The low, south-facing crag dries out early - often the first thing on Guye in condition - but the approach brush and boulder field may still hold snow.
climate.summer: Prime, though the south aspect bakes in the afternoon. Morning sessions climb far better than midday ones on a hot day.
climate.winter: Snowbound and out of condition; this side of the peak is also subject to ski-area avalanche control.
climate.typical: Marine west coast climate with heavy Pacific precipitation; west of the crest, temperatures very rarely fall below 0 F or exceed 80 F. Summer is comparatively dry and stable.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC Snoqualmie Pass zone (West Slopes Central); NOAA point forecast for Snoqualmie Pass

climate.typical: Marine west-coast climate — wet and cloudy, with fog frequently filling Gothic Basin even on days that are clear at the trailhead. The basin and summit gully can hold snow well into summer.

bySeason.summer: Best window is late July through September; June and early July usually still carry significant snow in the basin and summit gully (ice axe recommended). By August the route is typically mostly bare, loose talus.
bySeason.winter: Not a realistic winter objective — the Mountain Loop Highway is gated well below Barlow Pass, adding miles of road approach, and avalanche terrain guards the basin.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC "West Slopes North" zone (nearest official backcountry avalanche forecast for early/late-season snow travel).

climate.fall: Waterfall crossing dry and terrain largely snow-free through September, though snow can return by late October.
climate.spring: The route's waterfall/stream gully crossing can run medium-to-large, and terrain above the headwall remains avalanche-prone and icy.
climate.summer: Optimum climbing window (July-September); the waterfall gully crossing is typically low or entirely dry.
climate.winter: Avalanche-prone, icy terrain on the upper route; the waterfall/stream gully can run medium-to-large.
climate.typical: Marine west coast climate typical of the west-slope Cascades: high orographic precipitation, wet/heavy snow producing high avalanche danger in season, and temperatures that rarely fall below 0°F or exceed 80°F.
climate.forecastZone: West Slopes Central Cascades (Stevens Pass area) NWS zone forecast

climate.fall: September offers continued good conditions but increasing cloud cover and weather instability; snow possible by late September at higher elevations
climate.spring: Variable conditions April-May; lingering snow and wet conditions; avalanche danger moderate to high; transitions from winter to summer conditions unpredictably
climate.summer: Best climbing season. June-September: temperatures 50-70F daytime, 40-50F early morning/evening. Morning clear conditions typical, afternoon clouds/wind/thunderstorms common. Mossy/wet rock early season. Driest July-August.
climate.winter: November-March: Heavy snow, avalanche danger extreme, ice/mixed terrain. Avalanche blasting from ski resort. Temperatures 20-40F. Popular for winter mountaineering but very serious objective hazards.
climate.typical: Cool, wet maritime climate typical of Cascade Range. Temperatures range 40-70F in summer. Rapid weather changes common; afternoon thunderstorms and wind typical July-September.
climate.forecastZone: Northwest Avalanche Center - Snoqualmie Pass/Central Cascades Zone

climate.fall: Cooling but often stable dry spells continue through September before early-season snow returns.
climate.spring: Snow lingers on the approach into June; the access highway itself often isn't open until mid-to-late April.
climate.summer: Warm and dry; July-August are the most reliable snow-free months for climbing.
climate.winter: Highway closed; deep snow and avalanche terrain make this a non-objective in winter.
climate.typical: High, dry-summer East Cascades alpine climate: warm days with real afternoon thunderstorm potential and cold nights at this elevation; snow can linger in the approach gullies and shaded north notch into early-mid July.

bySeason.fall: Late-season (late Sep–Oct) can bring clear, stable weather but a shorter daylight window and colder nights; an early snowfall can end the season abruptly.
bySeason.summer: Jul-Sep is the reliable weather and snow-free window; check current conditions before early-July attempts.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC maintains a Washington Pass weather station for on-the-ground mountain weather; the area falls within NWS zone WAZ523 (Lower Slopes of the Eastern Washington Cascades Crest) for point forecasts.

climate.fall: Transitional and generally the worst time: thin snow over rock, verglas, and no consolidation. Trip reports from this window describe thin ice on rock and thin snow over slabs.
climate.spring: Prime season if the snowpack is stable - consolidated snow makes the gully fast - but this is also when wet-slide activity spikes on a south aspect. Climb early and get off before the day warms.
climate.summer: The gully melts out and the route becomes a dry easy-fifth-class scramble at about 800 ft to the south summit. Loose rock replaces snow as the main hazard.
climate.winter: The main season for the snow and mixed line, from roughly December through April. Firm, compacted approach conditions make it a half-day outing; heavy new snow makes it dangerous.
climate.typical: Marine west coast climate; Pacific fronts hitting the crest generate orographic lift and very heavy snowfall at the pass. Temperatures west of the crest very rarely fall below 0 F or exceed 80 F, which means rain-on-snow and rapid warming cycles are routine.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC Snoqualmie Pass avalanche forecast zone (West Slopes Central) - a mandatory read for this route
NWAC Snoqualmie Pass zone (nearest official avalanche/mountain weather forecast zone)

climate.typical: Marine west-coast climate typical of the North Cascades crest: frequent Pacific frontal precipitation (heaviest Nov–Mar) with a wet, dense snowpack; the Pickets hold snow late into the season on north-facing terrain, and approach gullies can remain snow-filled into July. Even in a good summer week, expect the possibility of afternoon cloud buildup and fast-moving weather off the Pacific.
climate.forecastZone: No NWAC avalanche forecast covers this zone in summer; use an NWS point forecast for the Mount Terror/Picket Range area (forecast.weather.gov) for current conditions.

climate.fall: Cool, stable spells in early October are excellent for the ridge scrambling, but hard-frozen cirque snow and the 15 October road shutdown close the window quickly.
climate.spring: Snow-covered and largely inaccessible until the road gate opens in mid-April, with deep snow on the north-facing approach into June. Wet avalanche hazard on cirque snow, high creek flows on Howlett Creek.
climate.summer: The season. June and July give continuous snow in the cirque; August and September give dry rock, less water and more loose ground. Wildfire smoke and closures are a recurring late-summer problem.
climate.winter: Not a practical objective. Road gated, deep unstable snow, verglassed chert, and a forested approach that would be a multi-day effort on skis or snowshoes.
climate.typical: Maritime North Cascades on the drier east side of the Skagit trench. Cold and windy at the summit even in midsummer; low-teens Celsius summit highs with freezing nights are typical in the climbing season.
climate.forecastZone: Mountain-Forecast Hozomeen Mountain summit forecast (2,458 m). No dedicated avalanche forecast zone; NWAC Mt Baker to the west and Avalanche Canada South Coast Inland to the north are the nearest, both extrapolation.

climate.fall: Early October can give crisp, stable rock weather with hard-frozen nights, but B.C.'s seasonal road shutdown around 15 October effectively ends the season.
climate.spring: Deep consolidating snow through June, and the best time for the north-side snow routes because the lower headwall is still filled in. Wet-slab and wet-loose avalanche hazard on the cirque snowfields in the afternoons, heavy runoff in the approach creeks, and the road often still gated.
climate.summer: July through September is the practical window. Ridges melt out by mid-July in a normal year and the rock routes want the driest settled weather available. Water becomes the limiting factor by August. Wildfire smoke and closures are common in late summer.
climate.winter: No practical access. The road gate is shut, the peak carries unstable maritime snow, and the chert verglasses. A winter ascent of Hozomeen has been a subject of long-running Cascade speculation rather than a normal objective.
climate.typical: Maritime North Cascades, but on the drier eastern flank of the Skagit trench. Pacific systems lose some moisture crossing the crest, so Hozomeen is drier than Baker and considerably wetter than the Methow. The summit runs cold and windy: mountain-forecast typically shows summit highs in the low teens Celsius with freezing nights even in the warm season.
climate.forecastZone: Mountain-Forecast publishes a dedicated Hozomeen Mountain summit forecast at 2,458 m. There is no dedicated avalanche forecast: NWAC's nearest US zone is Mt Baker and Avalanche Canada's South Coast Inland region borders from the north, so both are extrapolation for this peak.

climate.fall: A brief continuation of the late-summer window in early October, ended by cold, short days and the mid-October road closure. A wet fall shuts the route down immediately.
climate.spring: Wet, snowy and out of condition. The approach gully and rib traverse hold snow and the face runs with meltwater.
climate.summer: Late August into September is the window - the driest, most settled stretch, when the friable rock is at its most climbable and the approach is snow-free. Early summer is too wet.
climate.winter: Out of the question. No access, no conditions, and a wall of verglassed rotten rock.
climate.typical: Maritime North Cascades weather moderated slightly by position east of the crest. Summit conditions are cold and windy year-round; a west-facing wall stays in shade until afternoon.
climate.forecastZone: Mountain-Forecast Hozomeen Mountain summit forecast (2,458 m). No dedicated avalanche zone; NWAC Mt Baker and Avalanche Canada South Coast Inland are the nearest and are both extrapolation.

climate.fall: Climbable into September/early October with shortening days and increasing storm risk before the highway's winter closure.
climate.spring: Highway typically still gated or freshly reopened (mid-to-late April); snow and wet rock likely at the crag into early summer.
climate.summer: Best climbing window, late June through September; dry granite but watch for afternoon convective storms.
climate.winter: SR-20 is gated closed; the area is inaccessible by road.
climate.typical: Dry, warm alpine summers with afternoon thunderstorm risk; the shaded Ice Box stays notably cooler than sun-exposed Washington Pass faces.
climate.forecastZone: North Cascades / Washington Pass corridor (East Slopes Northern Cascades)

climate.fall: Shorter days; glaciers typically most melted-out and crevassed of the season.
climate.spring: Heavy lingering snowpack and higher avalanche hazard on the Ruth/Icy glacier slopes.
climate.summer: Main climbing window, though glacier snow cover reportedly degrades to bare ice on both glaciers as the season progresses.
climate.winter: Deep snow, road/trail access typically closed.
climate.typical: Maritime North Cascades climate: wet, snowy winters and drier but changeable summers; the Ruth and Icy Glaciers shrink progressively through the melt season.
climate.forecastZone: NWAC Mt. Baker zone

climate.typical: North Cascades receive some of the heaviest snowfall in the Lower 48; Icy Peak's glaciers and snowfields keep the route in reasonable climbing shape roughly mid-July through September. Expect fast-changing weather, frequent afternoon buildups/thunderstorms in late summer, and the possibility of new snow at any time above ~6,000 ft.

bySeason.fall: By October, cold nights and any early-season snowfall can make the summit gully icy and increase rockfall/avalanche hazard; most parties are done by late September.
bySeason.spring: The access road and lower trail may still hold snow into June after a normal winter; the Ruth Glacier approach can be climbable earlier for parties comfortable with full spring glacier travel, but crevasse bridges are less predictable.
bySeason.summer: Prime season (Jul-Sep). Early July retains more crevasse coverage/snow bridges on the Ruth Glacier (safer bridging but more hidden-crevasse risk); by September the Ruth-Icy col and Icy's approach slopes are mostly bare talus with more loose rock and less snow to cover awkward steps.

climate.forecastZone: NWAC 'Mt. Baker' zone for winter/spring avalanche forecasts (nwac.us); NWAC's daily avalanche forecast runs roughly Nov-Apr, so for summer glacier travel check the Mt. Baker Ranger District current-conditions page and recent trip reports instead.

climate.fall: September: Highs 61F decreasing to 50s, lows 39F to 30s. Increasing precipitation. October onwards: heavy rain, early snow possible.
climate.spring: May-early June: lingering snowpack, possible avalanche hazard, cold nights (30-40F)
climate.summer: June-August: best conditions. Highs 63-70F, lows 41-45F. Mornings clear, afternoon thunderstorms possible. Precipitation 1.7-2.2 inches monthly.
climate.winter: November-April: heavy snowpack, freezing temperatures. Not typically climbed.
climate.typical: Alpine climate with significant variability. Summer highs 60-70F, lows 40-50F. Afternoon thunderstorms common in July-August.
climate.forecastZone: Alpine Lakes Wilderness Zone, Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest
